abstract: Vladimir Asriyan (CREi, ICREA, BSE, CEPR), Hugo Reichardt (CREi, BSE, CEPR) and Sandro Shelegia (UPF, BSE, CEPR) ask what happens to long-run output when automation lands on the junior rungs of career ladders rather than on senior work. Their abstract: 'Early-career jobs often serve as stepping stones to more productive occupations later in life. Automating such jobs may disrupt skill accumulation. We study this possibility in an overlapping-generations economy with career ladders. Our main result is that automation of junior tasks can be immiserizing: when its cost savings are small, automation lowers long-run output. Immiseration occurs because junior automation shifts earnings to later in life. This shift lowers the present value of experience-intensive careers, so that fewer workers pursue them, and the supply of experienced workers falls. As the transition to the new steady state is Pareto efficient, any policy that averts immiseration hurts at least some workers. Incumbent experienced workers, for instance, benefit from higher senior wages without having suffered lower wages as juniors. In the context of U.S. robot automation, we provide empirical support for the theory's key predictions and explore its aggregate implications.' The model has two sectors: a modern sector where performing senior tasks requires prior experience in junior tasks, and a traditional sector requiring no experience. Workers sort by comparative advantage and smooth consumption through frictionless financial markets, so the immiseration result does not depend on credit constraints or labor market frictions. The paper is directly relevant to the jobsdata.ai early-career thesis because it supplies a supply-side mechanism, distinct from the demand-side substitution story in Brynjolfsson-Chandar-Chen, for why entry-level automation is not simply a transitional cost.
keyFindings: Empirical: 'an industry for which the junior bias was one standard deviation stronger saw an additional decline of about 10% in employment.' Effects appear after 1980 and are estimated on US Census and ACS microdata 1970-2020 at the 1990 Census industry classification.

Junior-biased robot exposure also predicts a rise in an industry's average worker age and a steepening of the wage-experience profile, both consistent with the model's transition path in which junior entry falls relative to the existing stock of seniors.

Calibrated to the 1980 US economy and evaluated at the Acemoglu-Restrepo (2020) estimate of roughly 30% robot cost savings, the model implies an output gain of about 2.6% against 3.5% under output maximization, so 'wage backloading thus dissipates around a quarter of the potential gain.'

Modern-sector output, the closest analogue to measured GDP, rises only about half a percentage point even at 30% cost savings, which the authors offer as an explanation for the 1980s-90s growth boom followed by stagnation.

At 30% cost savings the model predicts a 4.5 percentage-point fall in the labor force participation rate, against the observed rise in the share of 20-to-59-year-old men out of the labor force from 10.4% in 1980 to 15.0% in 2019.

The competitive equilibrium along the transition is Pareto efficient, so 'any policy that averts immiseration hurts at least some workers' - incumbent experienced workers gain higher senior wages without ever having absorbed lower junior wages.
methodology: Two-part paper. (1) Theory: an overlapping-generations model with career ladders and two sectors, frictionless labor and financial markets, CRRA preferences, and endogenous sorting into experience-intensive versus experience-free work. Calibration targets the US economy in 1980 (experience premium 88.7% from Lagakos et al. 2018; Frisch labor supply elasticity 0.75 from Chetty et al. 2011; 10.4% of 20-59-year-old men out of the labor force from the Census; 10% annualized real interest rate). Automatable junior and senior tasks are calibrated to match task-level robot exposure. (2) Empirics: industry-year panel from US Census and ACS microdata 1970-2020 on the 1990 Census industry classification. Junior bias is the correlation between age and occupation-level robot exposure within an industry, using LLM-constructed exposure measures from Garg et al. (2026); coefficients are normalized per standard deviation of junior bias. Regressions control for year and industry fixed effects and for the industry's overall robot exposure interacted with year, with 90% confidence intervals. Wage-growth tests use CPS matched consecutive-year earnings with standard errors clustered at the industry level. Robustness: junior-minus-senior exposure as an alternative independent variable, Webb (2019) exposure measures, and a 1990 rather than 1980 baseline.
qualifiers: The empirical evidence is about industrial robots between 1970 and 2020, not generative AI, and the authors present it as a test of the theory's mechanism rather than as an estimate of AI's effects. Coefficients are normalized per standard deviation of junior bias, so the ~10% employment figure has no direct translation into the jobsdata.ai early-career unit (percent employment decline for ages 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations versus least-exposed) - this is why the paper is recorded as an overlay rather than a plotted data point on every graph it touches. The model assumes frictionless labor and financial markets and no credit constraints, which strengthens the theoretical claim (immiseration does not require frictions) but limits its realism. Robot exposure comes from LLM-generated occupation ratings, a newer and less validated instrument than the Webb or IFR measures, though the paper reports a Webb replication. Working paper as of August 21, 2026; not yet peer reviewed. The Pareto-efficiency result is a property of the model's frictionless setup and should not be read as a general claim that no policy can improve on the automation transition.
